polls.finding: 43% of Massachusetts voters plan to vote yes on Question 3; WBUR calls it a tight contest.

pollingNote: Published polling on Question 3 reports the topline only. No public poll found tests which argument for it works, so a script's framing cannot be chosen from polling; it has to be tested.
opposition: Opponents argue a top-two primary can leave two candidates of the same party in November, favors self-funded candidates, and squeezes out third parties. Both major state parties and the AFL-CIO oppose it; supporters include officials of both parties and the NAACP.

consensus.title: Open primaries and Question 3
consensus.source: Statements from GovBlock's open-primaries conversation, plus the central claim of each library script

statements.text: Primaries paid for by taxpayers should be open to every registered voter.
A political party is a private association and should decide for itself who picks its nominees.
Independent voters are shut out of the only election that is actually competitive where they live.
Top-two primaries, where the two leading candidates advance regardless of party, produce better general elections.
Opening primaries would not make elected officials any less partisan.
The current system protects incumbents more than it protects parties.
Nonpartisan primaries would help good candidates who do not fit either party.
I would be more likely to vote in a primary if I did not have to register with a party.
Whatever the rule is, it should apply to every party in the state equally.
Most voters do not know their own state's primary rules, and that is the bigger problem.
When most races have only one name on the ballot, voters do not really have a choice.
Without competition there is no accountability.
Politicians who do not have to compete do not have to listen.
A top-two primary could leave two candidates of the same party on the November ballot, and that is a worse choice.
All-party primaries favor candidates who can pay for their own campaigns.
